entries.title: Who Moderates the Moderators?: A Law and Economics Approach to Holding Online Platforms Accountable Without Destroying the Internet
entries.subtitle: A proposal for conditioning Section 230's intermediary liability protections on reasonable efforts to curb unlawful content while maintaining Internet ecosystem viability.
entries.abstract: This paper examines the practical feasibility of reforming Section 230(c)(1) to impose indirect liability on online platforms for user-generated illegal or tortious content, contingent upon reasonable remedial measures. Drawing on law and economics analysis and common law precedents, the authors propose a duty-of-care standard with procedural safeguards designed to reduce harmful content without excessively burdening platforms or chilling speech. The paper systematically addresses common objections to Section 230 reform, contending that many concerns, while legitimate, are overstated or constitute arguments for broader procedural reform rather than defense of the statute itself.

entries.title: The Economics of Algorithmic Selection on the Internet
entries.subtitle: An examination of how algorithms shape information consumption, economic markets, and society while creating risks to privacy, fairness, and welfare
entries.abstract: This text discusses the pervasive role of algorithms in contemporary society, examining their function in shaping media consumption, influencing consumer behavior, and determining economic outcomes across various sectors. While algorithms provide essential organizational functions by filtering information and enabling new business models, they simultaneously create significant social and economic risks including manipulation, bias, privacy violations, and intellectual property concerns. The piece frames algorithmic systems as having both technofunctional utility and problematic impacts on economic and social welfare.

entries.title: Legal Policies on Platform Liability: An Economic Approach
entries.subtitle: An examination of platform liability policies and their economic implications for online marketplaces
entries.publisher: The Department of Economics of the Universitat de Barcelona
entries.abstract: This paper analyzes evolving platform liability policies in the United States and European Union, examining the economic implications of holding online platforms liable for harm from third-party seller transactions. The authors review relevant case law and regulatory frameworks including the 2022 Digital Services Act, 2024 Product Liability Directive, and 2019 ELI Model Rules. Using theoretical modeling, they assess how platform liability affects seller behavior, consumer welfare, and market efficiency, finding that increased liability can enhance consumer protection but may reduce seller safety investments for low-value goods. The authors propose subsidiary platform liability for significant harm and extended return policies to balance consumer protection with marketplace innovation.

entries.title: Platform Liability with Reputational Sanctions
entries.subtitle: An analysis of how legal liability imposed on monopoly platforms affects safety investments, consumer welfare, and seller participation.
entries.publisher: Department of Economics, Universitat de Barcelona, and Barcelona Economic Analysis Team (BEAT)
entries.abstract: This paper examines the interaction between platform legal liability, consumer reputation sanctions, and internal platform enforcement mechanisms in online marketplaces where a monopoly platform intermediates between sellers and consumers. The authors find that direct legal liability on platforms produces ambiguous effects on safety investments but generally increases overall welfare, except when legal costs are substantial. Furthermore, platform liability affects the composition of participating sellers differently depending on their heterogeneous sensitivities to consumer and platform sanctions, with the direction and magnitude of effects contingent on specific parameter values.

entries.title: PRODUCT LIABILITY AND ONLINE MARKETPLACES: COMPARISON AND REFORM
entries.subtitle: Examining the legal accountability of e-commerce platforms for defective products sold through their services across multiple jurisdictions.
entries.abstract: This article examines the applicability of traditional product liability doctrines to online marketplaces and e-commerce platforms. Through comparative analysis across multiple jurisdictions, the paper investigates whether online platforms can be held liable for defective products sold on their platforms and analyzes how product liability law has been adapted to address these challenges. The study evaluates the roles of both litigation and regulation, with particular focus on Europe and the United States, and proposes reforms to increase marketplace accountability.

entries.title: Holding Platforms Liable
entries.subtitle: An economic analysis of platform liability under conditions of firm solvency constraints and information asymmetry.
entries.abstract: This paper examines the economic rationale for imposing liability on digital platforms for harms caused by firms conducting transactions with users. The analysis demonstrates that when firms face limited liability constraints, platform liability creates incentives for platforms to increase interaction prices and invest in monitoring and enforcement mechanisms. The optimal level of platform liability depends critically on three factors: whether user participation requires explicit consent, the degree to which users bear the costs of harms, and the extent to which platform mitigation efforts are observable to regulators.

entries.title: Seller liability versus platform liability: optimal liability rule and law enforcement in the platform economy
entries.subtitle: An analysis of optimal liability allocation between platforms and sellers for intellectual property rights violations.
entries.publisher: European Journal of Law and Economics
entries.abstract: This paper examines the optimal allocation of liability for intellectual property right violations between e-commerce platforms and individual sellers. The authors distinguish between specific enforcement (where individual brand holders monitor only their own IP) and general enforcement (where platforms monitor all potential IP infringements). The analysis demonstrates that platform liability becomes socially preferable when the number of potential victims is large due to enforcement spillover effects. Using a two-seller model, the paper shows that seller liability with punitive damages calibrated to the enforcement probability can induce socially optimal outcomes, whereas platform liability may fail to achieve efficiency.

entries.title: The Economics of Two-Sided Markets
entries.abstract: This paper provides a comprehensive overview of two-sided markets, defined as markets in which two sets of agents interact through a platform or intermediary, and the decisions of each group affect the outcomes of the other through externalities. The paper explains the economic principles underlying two-sided markets, discusses firm strategies within such markets, and examines puzzling market outcomes. The work concludes by analyzing policy implications for antitrust and regulatory frameworks, with particular attention to recent issues in media, computer operating systems, and payment card industries.

entries.title: A Leverage Theory of Tying in Markets with Network Effects
entries.abstract: This paper develops a theoretical framework explaining how monopolists leverage unexploited consumer surplus through tying arrangements to establish quasi-installed base advantages in markets characterized by network effects. The analysis demonstrates that tying emerges as an optimal strategy without requiring precommitment, functioning as a mechanism that reduces the quality of competitors in tied markets. While tying may result in rival exclusion, it can simultaneously expand consumption of the tying product, generating ambiguous welfare implications for overall market efficiency.

entries.title: The Economics of Attention
entries.abstract: This paper synthesizes interdisciplinary research on attention from psychology and economics to explain documented violations of classical economic theory. The authors identify attention as a critical economic resource and examine emerging research directions including attention-based utility functions, attentional externalities created by digital technologies, artificial intelligence's impact on attention economics, and the role of motivational states such as boredom and curiosity in attention allocation.

entries.title: A Literature Review on the Theory of Asymmetric Information
entries.publisher: Advances in Economics, Management and Political Sciences
entries.abstract: This paper surveys historical literature on asymmetric information across diverse industries including lending, hospitality, and catering. The work examines how information asymmetries between market participants create problems such as adverse selection and moral hazard, reducing market efficiency and enabling poor resource allocation. The authors propose signaling and screening models as mechanisms to mitigate the negative effects of information asymmetry and promote greater market transparency and informed decision-making.

entries.title: The Global Landscape of Environmental AI Regulation: From the Cost of Reasoning to a Right to Green AI
entries.abstract: This paper examines the environmental impacts of generative AI systems, particularly Web search and reasoning models deployed in 2025, which demonstrate significantly higher cumulative environmental costs than previous AI generations. The authors map environmental regulatory frameworks across eleven jurisdictions, identifying limitations in current facility-level governance approaches that focus on training rather than inference and lack AI-specific energy disclosure requirements outside the EU. The paper proposes a three-pronged policy response including mandatory model-level transparency for inference consumption, user rights to opt out of unnecessary AI integration, and international coordination mechanisms to prevent regulatory arbitrage, with concrete legislative amendments to EU frameworks.

entries.title: Open-world evaluations for frontier AI progress
entries.subtitle: Proposes complementary qualitative evaluations of AI systems on real-world tasks beyond traditional benchmarks to better assess frontier capabilities.
entries.abstract: This paper argues that benchmark-based evaluation of AI systems has inherent limitations, as it privileges precisely specified, automatically gradable tasks that may not reflect real-world capability deployment. The authors advocate for open-world evaluationsÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂlong-horizon, messy real-world tasks assessed through qualitative analysisÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂas a complementary evaluation methodology. They introduce CRUX, a project for conducting regular open-world evaluations, and demonstrate the approach by tasking an AI agent with developing and publishing an iOS application, which was completed with minimal manual intervention. The work provides recommendations for designing and reporting open-world evaluations to identify emerging capabilities.

entries.title: Forecasting the Economic Effects of AI
entries.abstract: This study elicits probabilistic forecasts from five distinct groupsÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂacademic economists, AI company employees, AI policy researchers, superforecasters, and the general publicÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂregarding AI's impact on the U.S. economy. All groups expect substantial AI capability advances by 2030 and modest labor force participation declines, with median GDP growth forecasts of 2.5% exceeding baseline government projections. Under a rapid AI progress scenario, experts predict annualized GDP growth around 4% and labor force participation declining to 55% by 2050, with approximately 10 million jobs lost to AI. The study finds that expert disagreement stems primarily from differing beliefs about highly capable AI systems' economic effects rather than disagreement on AI progress timelines, and reveals substantial divergence in policy preferences, with experts favoring targeted interventions while the public supports both targeted and broad redistributive programs.

entries.title: Ethical Nudging
entries.abstract: This preliminary paper analyzes the ethical permissibility of government-deployed nudges as regulatory tools, arguing that their legitimacy depends on their effects on welfare, autonomy, and dignity. The author contends that many nudges that merit support enhance one or more of these values without undermining them. The analysis demonstrates that nudges can be ethically required on both welfare and autonomy grounds, while cautioning against manipulative applications such as dark patterns.

entries.title: Dynamic Pricing Algorithms, Consumer Harm, and Regulatory Response
entries.subtitle: An analysis of how algorithmic pricing creates consumer harm in competitive markets independent of collusion and proposes pricing regulation as a policy response.
entries.abstract: This article examines how pricing algorithms transform consumer markets across ride-sharing, travel, and retail sectors, arguing that algorithmic pricing poses broader policy challenges than collusive conduct alone. The author demonstrates that algorithmic pricing can generate higher consumer prices in competitive markets without explicit or tacit collusion, driven by the automated nature of algorithms and superior pricing technology deployed by individual firms. Drawing on historical precedent from early twentieth-century pricing innovation, the article proposes targeted pricing regulationÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂaddressing when and how firms set pricesÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂas a feasible policy solution, since antitrust law cannot address non-collusive algorithmic pricing harms.

entries.title: A Comprehensive Guide to Differential Privacy: From Theory to User Expectations
entries.subtitle: A comprehensive review of differential privacy frameworks, mechanisms, and applications for mitigating privacy risks in data-driven research.
entries.abstract: This survey provides a comprehensive examination of differential privacy (DP) as a mathematically grounded framework for addressing privacy concerns in data-intensive applications. The review covers theoretical foundations, practical mechanisms, and real-world applications across domains including machine learning and synthetic data generation. The paper identifies key algorithmic tools, domain-specific challenges, and usability issues, with emphasis on improving communication and transparency in DP system implementation to support responsible data use practices.

entries.title: The Constitutional Way of Thinking
entries.abstract: This paper examines several elements of "the constitutional way of thinking" beginning with a discussion of the commonality problem in patterns of thinking. Later sections address the productivity of reductionist classification schemes and how this is usefully applied to politics. More specifically, the discussion focuses first on why economists, in particular, have difficulty with this approach; second on the general problem of adhering to idealist thinking in political theory; and third on speculation into the conditions necessary to acquire "the constitutional way of thinking."

entries.title: Reranking Social Media Feeds: A Practical Guide for Field Experiments
entries.abstract: Social media plays a central role in shaping public opinion and behavior, yet performing experiments on these platforms and, in particular, on feed algorithms is becoming increasingly challenging. This guide offers practical recommendations for researchers developing and deploying field experiments focused on real-time reranking of social media feeds. The article is organized around two contributions. First, we provide an overview of an experimental method using web browser extensions that intercepts and reranks content in real time, enabling naturalistic reranking field experiments. We then describe feed interventions and measurements that this paradigm enables on participants' actual feeds, without requiring the involvement of social media platforms. Second, we offer concrete technical recommendations for intercepting and reranking social media feeds with minimal user-facing delay, and provide an open-source implementation. This document aims to summarize lessons learned in running field experiments on social media, provide concrete implementation details, and foster the ecosystem of independent social media research. Finally, we release the source code that serves as a blueprint for implementing future feed-ranking experiments.

entries.title: The Impossibility of a Paretian Liberal
entries.subtitle: An examination of the logical incompatibility between individual liberty and the Pareto principle in social choice theory.
entries.abstract: This paper presents an impossibility result demonstrating fundamental tensions between liberal principles of individual liberty and conventional social choice mechanisms. The authors formalize a minimalist concept of individual libertyÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂthe notion that individuals should retain absolute freedom over personal decisions regardless of majority preferenceÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂand prove its incompatibility with basic economic efficiency principles. The analysis reveals deep structural conflicts in constructing social decision rules that simultaneously respect both individual autonomy and collective welfare optimization.

entries.title: Social Choice and Individual Values, 1st ed.
entries.subtitle: An examination of the formal conditions required for aggregating individual preferences into rational collective social choices.
entries.publisher: Cowles Foundation for Research in Economics
entries.abstract: This text investigates whether it is formally possible to construct a procedure for transforming individual preferences into coherent social decision-making that satisfies basic rationality conditions. The author examines four methods of social choiceÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂvoting, market mechanisms, dictatorship, and conventionÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂand demonstrates through the paradox of voting that majority preference aggregation fails to produce transitive collective preferences. The study questions whether any method of aggregating diverse individual tastes can produce rational collective behavior, establishing foundational questions for social choice theory.

entries.title: DNA as a universal chemical substrate for computing and data storage
entries.abstract: DNA computing and DNA data storage represent emerging paradigms that leverage DNA molecules as computing substrates and storage media, offering nanoscale compactness and operation in unconventional aqueous environments. This review explores the integration of DNA computing with neural networks and compartmentalized DNA circuits, as well as strategies for writing, reading, retrieving, and editing DNA-encoded data. The work bridges DNA computing and data storage fields and examines applications of DNA-based near-memory computing for future information technology and health analysis.

entries.title: A Definition of AGI
entries.subtitle: Introduces a quantifiable framework for AGI grounded in Cattell-Horn-Carroll theory, defining AGI as matching the cognitive versatility and proficiency of a well-educated adult.
entries.abstract: The lack of a concrete definition for Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) obscures the gap between today's specialized AI and human-level cognition. This paper introduces a quantifiable framework to address this, defining AGI as matching the cognitive versatility and proficiency of a well-educated adult. To operationalize this, we ground our methodology in Cattell-Horn-Carroll theory, the most empirically validated model of human cognition. The framework dissects general intelligence into ten core cognitive domains ÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂ including reasoning, memory, and perception ÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂ and adapts established human psychometric batteries to rigorously evaluate AI systems. Applying this framework, we find that today's frontier AI models exhibit high but uneven performance, with notable weaknesses in specific cognitive domains.

entries.title: Audits Under Resource, Data, and Access Constraints: Scaling Laws For Less Discriminatory Alternatives
entries.subtitle: Examines how auditors can identify less discriminatory algorithmic alternatives under realistic constraints on data, compute, and model access.
entries.abstract: AI audits play a critical role in AI accountability and safety. One branch of the law for which AI audits are particularly salient is anti-discrimination law. Several areas of anti-discrimination law implicate the 'less discriminatory alternative' (LDA) requirement, in which a defendant may be liable if a similarly effective but less discriminatory alternative exists. This paper examines how auditors can identify less discriminatory alternatives under realistic constraints on data, compute, and model access, and derives scaling laws governing the relationship between audit resources and the probability of successfully identifying such alternatives.

entries.title: On Goodhart's Law, with an Application to Value Alignment
entries.subtitle: Formalizes Goodhart's Law and applies it to the value alignment problem, showing that optimizing proxy measures of human values tends to undermine the values themselves.
entries.abstract: "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure." This paper formalizes Goodhart's Law and applies it to the problem of value alignment in AI systems. The authors show that when an AI system is trained to optimize a proxy measure of human values, the resulting system tends to undermine the values the proxy was meant to capture. The paper derives conditions under which alignment by proxy fails and discusses implications for the design of reward functions and evaluation frameworks.

entries.title: The Coasean Singularity? Demand, Supply, and Market Design with AI Agents
entries.subtitle: Applies Coasean theory of the firm to AI agents, arguing that sufficiently capable agents collapse transaction costs and reorganize markets around new equilibria.
entries.abstract: AI agentsÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂautonomous systems that perceive, reason, and act on behalf of human principalsÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂ¢ÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂÃÂare poised to transform digital markets by dramatically reducing transaction costs. This chapter evaluates the economic implications of this transition, adopting a consumer-oriented view of agents as market participants that can search, negotiate, and transact directly. From the demand side, agent adoption reflects derived demand: users trade off decision quality against effort reduction, with outcomes mediated by agent capability and task context. On the supply side, firms will design, integrate, and monetize agents, with outcomes hinging on whether agents operate within or across platforms. At the market level, agents create efficiency gains from lower search, communication, and contracting costs, but also introduce frictions such as congestion and price obfuscation. By lowering the costs of preference elicitation, contract enforcement, and identity verification, agents expand the feasible set of market designs but also raise novel regulatory challenges. While the net welfare effects remain an empirical question, the rapid onset of AI-mediated transactions presents a unique opportunity for economic research to inform real-world policy and market design.

entries.title: An Economy of AI Agents
entries.subtitle: Surveys how AI agents capable of planning and executing complex tasks may reshape markets, organizations, and the institutions required for well-functioning economies.
entries.abstract: In the coming decade, artificially intelligent agents with the ability to plan and execute complex tasks over long time horizons with little direct oversight from humans may be deployed across the economy. This chapter surveys recent developments and highlights open questions for economists around how AI agents might interact with humans and with each other, shape markets and organizations, and what institutions might be required for well-functioning markets.

entries.title: A Note on Human Capital, the Division of Labor, and Artificial Intelligence
entries.subtitle: Argues that AI has a comparative advantage in coordination tasks, which deepens human specialization rather than replacing specialists.
entries.publisher: Peter Isztin / Corvinus University of Economics
entries.abstract: This paper considers the effects of generative artificial intelligence tools on the division of labor. Following Becker and Murphy (1992), the author posits a team with each member assigned to a task. Specialization is limited not only by the extent of the market, but also by coordination costs, which include the need for knowledge in multiple tasks. AI helps the coordination of the team by being a substitute for human generalist knowledge, resulting in a greater number of specialized fields. The introduction of AI also increases the return to knowledge that is equally productive in all tasks. The paper shows that AI agents would typically have a comparative advantage in coordinating specialists, while human agents perform specialist roles.
